name: Place Outa el Hammam
hero_subtitle: The lively heart of the blue city, ringed by cafés, a red-walled Kasbah and the Grand Mosque.

overview.title: The Square Where Chefchaouen Meets
overview.p1: Place Outa el Hammam is the main square of the medina and the easiest place to get your bearings. On one side stands the red-walled Kasbah, on the other the Grand Mosque with its unusual octagonal minaret, and in between a row of cafés and restaurants spilling onto the cobbles.
overview.p2: It is a place to sit rather than to tick off. Order a mint tea, watch locals and travellers drift past, and let the light change on the walls. Mornings are calm, evenings are busier, and the square works as the starting point for almost every walk in the medina. Non-Muslim visitors can't enter the mosque, but the exterior is worth a look.

moods.title: What to Do at Place Outa el Hammam
moods.subtitle: Easy pleasures, all within a few steps.

1.title: Mint Tea on the Terrace
1.desc: Pick a table facing the Kasbah and stay a while. It is the classic way to see the square.

2.title: The Kasbah Next Door
2.desc: The fortress and its gardens are right on the square, so it makes sense to combine the two.

3.title: Starting Point for Walks
3.desc: Alleys to Al Souika, Ras El Maa and the Spanish Mosque path all begin nearby. Set off here.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Place Outa el Hammam

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: The medina is car-free. Taxis stop at the gates, so walk in from there; the square is a few minutes uphill.

2.title: Timing
2.desc: Mornings are calm and good for photos; evenings are lively. Weekends and holidays are busiest.

3.title: Good to Know
3.desc: Check prices on the menu before ordering. ATMs are near the square, and most small places take cash only.

q1.question: Where is Place Outa el Hammam?
q1.answer: It is the main square in the heart of Chefchaouen's medina, next to the Kasbah and the Grand Mosque.

q2.question: What is the best time to visit Place Outa el Hammam?
q2.answer: Late afternoon and early evening, when the light is soft and the cafés fill up.

q3.question: Can I enter the Grand Mosque?
q3.answer: No. Non-Muslim visitors cannot enter, but you can admire the minaret and exterior from the square.

q4.question: How long should I spend on the square?
q4.answer: One to two hours is plenty, including a tea and the Kasbah next door.
